title: Amino Acids: How One Side Chain Decides Everything

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In Pauling's electrophoresis experiment, hemoglobin from healthy people and from people with sickle-cell anemia was placed in an electric field at the same pH, and the two moved differently. What does that result show?
cards.back: At the same pH the two hemoglobins carry different net charges. For molecules of the same size and shape, only a charge difference explains different movement.
cards.quote: For two molecules of the same size and shape, only a charge difference explains that.

cards.front: The alpha-carbon of an amino acid carries four groups: an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a side chain, the {{c1::R group}}.
cards.back: The R group carries the differences: size, charge, comfort in water, reactivity.
cards.quote: carrying four groups: an amino group (written −NH₂), a carboxyl group (written −COOH), a hydrogen, and a side chain, the R group.
cards.section: One backbone, twenty side chains

cards.front: Why are 19 of the 20 amino acids chiral, while glycine is not?
cards.back: Chirality needs four different groups on the alpha-carbon. Glycine's R group is just another hydrogen, so its alpha-carbon carries two identical groups and it is achiral.
cards.quote: The exception is glycine, whose R group is just another hydrogen, so it is the only achiral amino acid.
cards.section: One backbone, twenty side chains

cards.front: Proteins are built almost exclusively from the {{c1::L}} form of the chiral amino acids.
cards.back: L and D are non-superimposable mirror images, like your two hands.
cards.quote: Proteins are built almost exclusively from the L form.
cards.section: One backbone, twenty side chains

cards.front: Why does glycine turn up so often in tight turns of a protein backbone?
cards.back: Its tiny side chain (a hydrogen) lets it take backbone angles that other residues cannot.
cards.quote: That tiny side chain lets it take backbone angles other residues cannot, so it turns up in tight turns.
cards.section: One backbone, twenty side chains

cards.front: The pKa of an ionizable group is the pH at which {{c1::half}} of those groups hold a proton.
cards.quote: Each switch has a set point, its pKa: the pH at which half of those groups hold a proton.
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: For a free amino acid in water, what does an ionizable group mostly do below its pKa, and above it? How fast does the balance change?
cards.back: Below its pKa it mostly holds its proton; above it, it mostly lets go. Each pH unit away from the pKa makes the winning form ten times more common.
cards.quote: Below a group's pKa it mostly holds its proton; above it the group mostly lets go.
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: Why does "deprotonated" not always mean "negative" for an ionizable group?
cards.back: Holding a proton always makes a group one charge more positive. Acid-type groups go from 0 to −1 when they lose H⁺, but base-type groups go from +1 to 0, so a deprotonated lysine side chain is neutral.
cards.quote: So "deprotonated" does not mean "negative": a lysine side chain that has lost its proton is neutral.
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: Glutamate's side-chain carboxyl has a pKa of 4.25. At blood pH 7.4, about how many side chains are deprotonated for every one protonated, and what is the side chain's charge?
cards.back: 7.4 − 4.25 = 3.15 units above the pKa; 10^3.15 ≈ 1400 to one. Over 99% have let go, so the side chain is negative for all practical purposes.
cards.quote: Glutamate's side chain at blood pH: 7.4 − 4.25 = 3.15 units, more than two, so over 99% have let go
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: Free histidine's imidazole side chain has a pKa of about 6.0. At pH 7.4, roughly what percentage of these side chains are positive?
cards.back: 7.4 − 6.0 = 1.4; 10^1.4 ≈ 25 neutral for every 1 positive, so about 1/26 ≈ 4% positive.
cards.quote: About 25 are neutral for every one that is positive, so it is about 4% positive.
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log({{c1::[A⁻]/[HA]}}).
cards.back: [A⁻] is the deprotonated form and [HA] the protonated form.
cards.quote: Textbooks and the MCAT write the same equation as pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: Glycine has two switches: carboxyl pKa₁ = 2.34 and amino pKa₂ = 9.60. Predict its net charge at pH 1, pH 6 and pH 12.
cards.back: About +1, 0 and about −1. At pH 1 both hold protons (−COOH 0, −NH₃⁺ +1); at pH 6 −COO⁻ (−1) and −NH₃⁺ (+1); at pH 12 −COO⁻ (−1) and −NH₂ (0).
cards.quote: Glycine has just the two backbone switches: carboxyl pKa₁ = 2.34 and amino pKa₂ = 9.60.
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: What is a zwitterion, and does the term mean net charge zero?
cards.back: A molecule carrying both a positive and a negative charge. It does not mean net zero: aspartate at pH 7.4 has both charges and is net −1.
cards.quote: A molecule carrying both a positive and a negative charge is a zwitterion (which does not mean net zero
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: Why is free glycine almost entirely the net-zero zwitterion at blood pH, about 7.4?
cards.back: 7.4 lies well between pKa₁ (2.34) and pKa₂ (9.60): the carboxyl has let go and the amino group holds on. The zwitterion is over 90% of glycine from about pH 3.3 to 8.6, one unit inside each pKa.
cards.quote: Glycine's net-zero zwitterion is more than 90% of it from about pH 3.3 to 8.6, one unit inside each pKa.
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which a molecule's net charge is exactly {{c1::zero}}.
cards.back: It is the average of the two pKa values on either side of the net-zero rung.
cards.quote: The pH where the net charge is exactly zero is the isoelectric point, pI
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: Why is the pI of glycine the average of its two pKa values?
cards.back: Near the pI almost all glycine is zwitterion, plus a little +1 and a little −1 form. Net zero needs equal amounts of those two: 10^(pKa₁ − pH) = 10^(pH − pKa₂), so pH = (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2.
cards.quote: Near the pI almost all glycine is the zwitterion, with a little +1 and a little −1 form, and zero net charge needs equal amounts of those two.
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: Calculate the pI of glycine (pKa₁ = 2.34, pKa₂ = 9.60).
cards.back: The net-zero form sits between the two pKa values: pI = (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97.
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: Aspartate has three switches: backbone carboxyl 1.88, side-chain carboxyl 3.65, backbone amino 9.60. Find its net charge at pH 7.4 and its pI.
cards.back: At 7.4: −1 (both carboxyls −1, amino +1). Ladder: +1 below 1.88, 0 past 1.88, −1 past 3.65, −2 past 9.60. Net-zero rung lies between 1.88 and 3.65, so pI = (1.88 + 3.65)/2 = 2.77.
cards.why: Averaging the two backbone values (5.74) is the common error; aspartate carries −1 there, not 0. Find the net-zero rung first.
cards.quote: The net-zero rung sits between 1.88 and 3.65, so pI = (1.88 + 3.65) / 2 = 2.77.
cards.section: Proton switches: the one rule for charge

cards.front: Why are the Asp and Glu side chains negative at pH 7.4?
cards.back: They are acid-type switches with pKa near 4, far below 7.4, so they have let go of their protons: −COO⁻, charge −1.
cards.quote: Acid-type switches near pKa 4, far below 7.4, so they have let go: negative.
cards.section: Four side-chain families, read from the switches

cards.front: Histidine is classed as a basic amino acid. Is free histidine's side chain mostly charged at pH 7.4, and why is it grouped with the bases?
cards.back: No, it is mostly neutral at 7.4 because its switch sits near 6. It is a base-type switch, so it is grouped with the bases by convention.
cards.quote: His is a base whose switch sits near 6, so free histidine is mostly neutral at 7.4
cards.section: Four side-chain families, read from the switches

cards.front: Free lysine has a backbone carboxyl (pKa about 2), a backbone amino group (8.95) and a side-chain amino group (10.53). Predict its net charge at pH 7.4.
cards.back: +1. The carboxyl has let go (−1); both amino groups sit above 7.4 and hold their protons (+1 each).
cards.quote: Lys and Arg switches sit far above 7.4, so they hold on: positive.
cards.section: Four side-chain families, read from the switches

cards.front: Name the polar, uncharged amino acids and the group each carries.
cards.back: Hydroxyls: Ser, Thr, Tyr. Amides: Asn, Gln. Thiol: Cys (reactive).
cards.quote: The hydroxyls of Ser, Thr and Tyr, the amides of Asn and Gln, and the reactive thiol of Cys.
cards.section: Four side-chain families, read from the switches

cards.front: Where do hydrophobic side chains (Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Met, Pro, Phe, Trp) sit in a folded protein, and why?
cards.back: They tend to bury themselves in the protein's core, away from water (and are at home facing lipid). They are greasy hydrocarbon or aromatic chains with no switch, so they are not comfortable in water.
cards.quote: Greasy hydrocarbon and aromatic chains with no switch, which bury themselves in a protein's core, away from water.
cards.section: Four side-chain families, read from the switches

cards.front: What is a salt bridge, and which side chains form them?
cards.back: An ion pair between opposite charges: Asp and Glu (negative) with Lys and Arg (positive).
cards.quote: include the residues that form salt bridges, ion pairs between opposite charges (Asp and Glu with Lys and Arg)
cards.section: Four side-chain families, read from the switches

cards.front: In a membrane-spanning helix, a lipid-facing leucine is replaced with lysine. Is the new residue at home there, and why?
cards.back: No. Lysine is positive at pH 7.4, and the lipid interior has no water, so a charged side chain is out of place there while a greasy one like leucine is at home.
cards.quote: the lipid interior has no water, so charged and polar side chains are out of place and greasy ones are at home
cards.section: Four side-chain families, read from the switches

cards.front: On a titration curve with well-separated pKa values, where does each pKa sit?
cards.back: At the middle of a flat part (buffering region), the half-equivalence point.
cards.quote: For well-separated pKa values, each pKa sits at the middle of a flat part, the half-equivalence point.
cards.section: Reading the curve: titration, pKa and pI

cards.front: Why does the pH barely change across a flat part of an amino acid's titration curve?
cards.back: It is a buffering region: one switch is busy letting go of its protons, so the added base is used up there and barely moves the pH.
cards.quote: Each flat part is a buffering region, where added base barely moves the pH because one switch is busy letting go of its protons.
cards.section: Reading the curve: titration, pKa and pI

cards.front: Why does glycine's pI (5.97) fall in a steep jump of its titration curve rather than a flat part?
cards.back: Its two pKa values (2.34 and 9.60) are far apart. At 5.97 no switch is mid-change, so almost every molecule is the net-zero form and nothing buffers.
cards.quote: the pI of 5.97 sits in the steep jump between them: no switch is mid-change there, so almost every molecule is the net-zero form and nothing buffers
cards.section: Reading the curve: titration, pKa and pI

cards.front: Histidine's pKa values are 1.82 (carboxyl), 6.00 (imidazole) and 9.17 (amino). Calculate its pI.
cards.back: Ladder: +2, +1 past 1.82, 0 past 6.00, −1 past 9.17. The net-zero rung lies between 6.00 and 9.17: pI = (6.00 + 9.17)/2 ≈ 7.59.
cards.quote: Histidine, with its extra imidazole switch, has three (pKa₁ = 1.82, pKa₂ = 6.00, pKa₃ = 9.17) and a pI of 7.59.
cards.section: Reading the curve: titration, pKa and pI

cards.front: Lysine's two pKa values on either side of its net-zero form are 8.95 and 10.53. Calculate its pI, then predict which electrode free lysine moves toward in electrophoresis at pH 7.4.
cards.back: pI = (8.95 + 10.53)/2 = 9.74. At pH 7.4, below its pI, lysine is net positive and moves toward the cathode.
cards.why: Rests on two rules: pI is the average of the pKa values bracketing the net-zero rung, and below its pI a molecule is net positive and moves to the cathode.
cards.quote: When the two are close, as in aspartate (1.88 and 3.65) or lysine (8.95 and 10.53), their flat parts merge
cards.section: Reading the curve: titration, pKa and pI

cards.front: A protein pocket raises a histidine's imidazole pKa from 6.0 to 7.0. What share of these side chains is protonated at pH 7.4?
cards.back: pKa − pH = −0.4; 10^−0.4 ≈ 0.40 protonated per neutral, so 0.40/1.40 ≈ 28% (up from about 4%). At pKa 7.4 it would be half and half.
cards.quote: Raise the imidazole pKa from 6.0 to 7.0, as a protein pocket can, and the protonated share at pH 7.4 goes from about 4% to about 28%
cards.section: Reading the curve: titration, pKa and pI

cards.front: Why is histidine the residue enzymes use most often to pass protons in active sites?
cards.back: A residue that must give and take protons works best with its pKa near the enzyme's working pH, and histidine's neutral-to-positive switch sits near there.
cards.quote: a residue that must give and take protons works best with its pKa near the enzyme's working pH.
cards.section: Reading the curve: titration, pKa and pI

cards.front: A hypothetical mutation in an enzyme pocket shifts its active-site histidine's imidazole pKa from 6.0 down to 4.0. At pH 7.4, predict the protonated share and the effect on its work as a proton shuttle.
cards.back: About 0.04% protonated (10^−3.4 ≈ 1 in 2500). It is almost always neutral, so it rarely toggles at the working pH and becomes a poor shuttle.
cards.why: Rests on the tenfold-per-unit rule and on the rule that a proton-passing residue works best with its pKa near the enzyme's working pH.
cards.quote: But histidine's neutral-to-positive switch is the one enzymes use most to pass protons
cards.section: Reading the curve: titration, pKa and pI

cards.front: In electrophoresis, which way does a molecule move below its pI, above its pI, and at its pI?
cards.back: Below pI: net positive, to the cathode (negative electrode). Above pI: to the anode (positive electrode). At pI: it stays put.
cards.quote: Below its pI a molecule is net positive and moves to the cathode; above its pI it moves to the anode; at its pI it stays put.
cards.section: Electrophoresis: which way does it move?

cards.front: In an electrophoresis buffer at pH 6.0, predict which way glycine (pI 5.97), aspartate (pI 2.77) and histidine (pI 7.59) move.
cards.back: Glycine barely moves (pH is almost its pI). Aspartate, far above its pI, is about −1 and moves toward the anode. Histidine, below its pI, is about +0.5 and moves toward the cathode.
cards.why: With the imidazole pKa at 6.0, half the histidine side chains are protonated at pH 6.0.
cards.quote: In a buffer at pH 6.0, which way do glycine (pI 5.97), aspartate (pI 2.77) and histidine (pI 7.59) move?
cards.section: Electrophoresis: which way does it move?

cards.front: Sickle-cell hemoglobin (HbS) has valine in place of glutamate at position 6 of each beta chain. How does its net charge per molecule compare with normal HbA at pH 7.4?
cards.back: Glutamate's side chain is −1 at 7.4; valine has no switch. Each of the two beta chains loses one negative charge, so HbS is +2 per molecule relative to HbA.
cards.quote: Each of hemoglobin's two beta chains loses one negative charge, so HbS is +2 per molecule relative to normal hemoglobin (HbA).
cards.section: The payoff: one swap, two properties

cards.front: HbA and HbS are run on a gel in an alkaline buffer, where hemoglobin is net negative. Which runs faster toward the anode, and why?
cards.back: HbA. Both are net negative, but HbS carries two fewer negative charges per molecule, so it moves more slowly toward the anode.
cards.quote: In an alkaline buffer, where hemoglobin is net negative, HbA runs toward the anode faster than HbS.
cards.section: The payoff: one swap, two properties

cards.front: Hemoglobin C replaces the same beta-chain glutamate with lysine. Predict its charge change per molecule versus HbA, its gel position relative to HbA and HbS, and whether it forms sickle fibers.
cards.back: +4 per molecule (+2 per chain), twice HbS's change; toward the anode the order is HbA, HbS, HbC. It does not form sickle fibers: lysine, like glutamate, is charged and hydrophilic, so it plants no greasy patch.
cards.why: Charge sets gel position; polarity sets sickling. HbC forms crystals and causes a much milder anemia.
cards.quote: Lysine, like glutamate, is charged and hydrophilic, so it plants no greasy patch.
cards.section: The payoff: one swap, two properties

cards.front: Why does the Glu→Val swap at beta position 6 make red cells sickle?
cards.back: Hydrophobic valine plants a greasy patch on the water-facing surface. When hemoglobin gives up oxygen, a matching hydrophobic pocket opens; one molecule's valine patch sticks into the next, chaining hemoglobin into rigid fibers that deform the cell.
cards.quote: The valine patch of one molecule sticks into that pocket on the next, chaining hemoglobin into rigid fibers that deform the red cell into a sickle.
cards.section: The payoff: one swap, two properties

cards.front: A hypothetical hemoglobin variant replaces the beta-6 glutamate with glutamine, a polar side chain with no switch. Predict its gel behavior compared with HbS, and whether the lesson's rules predict sickling.
cards.back: Charge: like HbS, each beta chain loses one negative charge, so +2 per molecule and the same gel shift. Sickling: not predicted, because glutamine is polar and plants no greasy patch.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's split: charge explains the gel, polarity explains sickling.
cards.quote: So charge explains how Pauling saw the defect; polarity explains why the cells sickle.
cards.section: The payoff: one swap, two properties

cards.front: By the CORN rule, an amino acid is viewed with its alpha-carbon hydrogen pointing away from you, and CO → R → N traces clockwise. Is it L or D?
cards.back: D. With H toward you, clockwise reads L; viewing from the other side flips the handedness.
cards.quote: Clockwise reads L, counterclockwise D; view from the other side and the handedness flips.
cards.section: Assigning L and D: the CORN rule

cards.front: In R/S terms, what is the configuration of L amino acids?
cards.back: S for every chiral amino acid except cysteine, which is R because of its sulfur-bearing side chain.
cards.quote: In R/S terms, L is S for every chiral amino acid except cysteine, whose sulfur-bearing side chain makes it R.
cards.section: Assigning L and D: the CORN rule

cards.front: Thalidomide's two mirror-image forms are thought to carry different effects (sedation versus birth defects). Why would giving only the pure "safe" form not have been safe?
cards.back: The body converts each form into the other within hours.
cards.quote: Because the body converts each form into the other within hours, even the pure "safe" form would not have been safe.
cards.section: Thalidomide

cards.front: Why can the pKa of a side chain inside a protein differ from its value in a free amino acid?
cards.back: The local environment can shift a pKa substantially: a buried Asp or a Lys in a hydrophobic pocket can move several pH units, and histidine's is often shifted nearer to 7.
cards.quote: A protein's local environment can shift a pKa substantially: a buried Asp or a Lys in a hydrophobic pocket can move several pH units
cards.section: pKa values inside proteins

cards.front: Suppose a protein pocket shifts a buried aspartate side chain's pKa to 7.4. Predict its average charge at pH 7.4 and what new role this makes possible.
cards.back: Half the side chains hold a proton, so the average charge is about −0.5. Like a histidine at pKa 7.4, it could then give or take a proton at that pH, the basis of pH-dependent catalysis.
cards.why: Rests on the pKa definition (half protonated at pH = pKa) and the rule that proton-passing works best with pKa near the working pH.
cards.quote: Such shifts underlie pH-dependent catalysis and shape changes.
cards.section: pKa values inside proteins

cards.front: Free cysteine's thiol has a pKa of about 8.2. What share is thiolate (deprotonated) at pH 7.4, and does cysteine normally form salt bridges?
cards.back: 8.2 − 7.4 = 0.8; 10^0.8 ≈ 6.3 neutral per thiolate, so about 1/7.3 ≈ 14% thiolate (86% neutral). It is mostly neutral, so it does not normally form salt bridges.
cards.quote: At pH 7.4 tyrosine's side chain is about 99.8% neutral and free cysteine's about 86% (14% thiolate), so neither normally forms salt bridges.
cards.section: Small print on the numbers

cards.front: Which stain reveals amino acids after chromatography, and what color does it give?
cards.back: Ninhydrin stains free alpha-amino groups purple; proline turns yellow.
cards.quote: ninhydrin stains free alpha-amino groups purple (proline turns yellow) so each spot shows.
cards.section: Detecting amino acids in the lab
